_note: Batch 6 — the remaining 38 concepts, closing that bucket. Delay and space, phase and stereo, saturation, mastering, and the low end. The phase entries matter most: phase is the one area where a producer can make a mix measurably worse while every individual decision sounds fine.

questions.q: What is a tilt EQ?
questions.short: One control that raises one end of the spectrum while lowering the other, pivoting around a centre.
steps: Use it on a mix bus or a bus for a quick brighter-or-warmer decision.
Set the pivot around 500 Hz–1 kHz for a whole-mix tilt.
Keep it to 1–2 dB; a tilt affects everything, so it adds up fast.
Use it to A/B a direction before committing to specific bands.
questions.why: A tilt is two broad shelves moving in opposite directions, so it changes the balance between low and high without changing the total energy much. That makes it good for deciding a direction quickly and poor for fixing anything specific.
questions.watch: Tilting to fix a dull mix also thins the low end. Check the bass before you accept it.

questions.q: How many EQ bands is too many?
questions.short: If you need more than four on one source, the problem is the recording or the arrangement.
steps: Expect one filter and two or three bands on most sources.
If you are at six bands, bypass them all and listen again — some are cancelling each other.
Ask whether the next band is fixing the source or fixing a conflict with another track.
Consider re-recording, swapping the sample, or changing the arrangement instead.
questions.why: Each band is a response to a problem, so a long chain of them usually means the problems are being treated rather than solved. A source needing eight corrections is a source that was captured wrong or is in the wrong place in the arrangement.
questions.watch: Mastering and complex live recordings are legitimate exceptions. A single mic on a single instrument is not.

questions.q: Why does reverb make my mix muddy?
questions.short: The tail has low mids in it, and a tail lasts far longer than the source that triggered it.
steps: High-pass every reverb return at 250–400 Hz.
Low-pass at 7–10 kHz so the tail adds no hiss.
Shorten the decay until it ends before the next chord change.
Add pre-delay so the dry signal arrives clear of the tail.
Use fewer reverbs — one shared space beats five private ones.
questions.why: A source might occupy 200–400 Hz for half a second; its reverb occupies the same band for two. Summed across six sources, the low mids are continuously filled by tails even though no individual source sounds muddy.
questions.watch: Reverb mud is invisible in solo, because in solo the tail has nothing to be muddy with.

questions.q: What is a slapback delay and where does it belong?
questions.short: A single repeat at 60–140 ms with no feedback. It adds depth without the wash of reverb.
steps: One repeat, 60–140 ms, feedback at zero.
Set the level low — you should notice it when muted, not when playing.
Filter it: high-pass at 400 Hz, low-pass at 5 kHz.
Use it on vocals, guitars and snares where reverb would cloud the mix.
At the short end it thickens; at the long end it becomes an audible echo.
questions.why: A single early reflection is the simplest depth cue there is, and it adds a fraction of the energy that a reverb tail does. That is why it works in dense mixes where any reverb would immediately cloud the low mids.
questions.watch: Slapback on a fast delivery smears the words. Shorten it or drop the level.

questions.q: What is ping-pong delay and when does it hurt the mix?
questions.short: Repeats alternating left and right. Beautiful on a sparse mix, chaos on a busy one.
steps: Use it when there is space — intros, breakdowns, sparse verses.
Keep feedback low, two or three audible repeats at most.
High-pass the return at 400 Hz so the bouncing does not carry low mids around.
Automate it on for one line rather than leaving it on the whole song.
Check mono: ping-pong collapses to a plain delay, which may be louder than you expect.
questions.why: Alternating repeats draw attention because the ear tracks movement in the stereo field. In a sparse arrangement that is the effect you want; in a dense one it adds a moving element competing with everything already there.
questions.watch: In mono the two sides sum, so a tasteful ping-pong can be twice as loud on a phone.

questions.q: How do I set delay feedback?
questions.short: Count the audible repeats, not the percentage. Two or three for rhythm, one for depth.
steps: Set the level first, then the feedback, listening for how many repeats you can actually hear.
Two to three repeats keeps it rhythmic; more becomes a wash.
Filter the feedback path so each repeat gets darker, like a real echo.
High feedback plus a tempo-synced time is a texture, not a delay — treat it as such.
Automate feedback up for one throw rather than leaving it high.
questions.why: Feedback is how much of the output is returned to the input, so it compounds: 50% gives a long tail, 70% nearly never decays. What matters perceptually is the number of repeats above the noise floor of the mix, which depends on the delay's level as much as its feedback.
questions.watch: Feedback above about 85% can self-oscillate and build to full scale. Watch your meters.

questions.q: How do I make delays sit behind the vocal?
questions.short: Filter them, duck them under the dry vocal, and time them to land in the gaps.
steps: High-pass the delay return at 400–600 Hz and low-pass at 4–6 kHz.
Duck the return 3–4 dB whenever the dry vocal is present.
Choose a delay time that lands between words, not on them — dotted eighth usually works.
Keep the first repeat quieter than you think; you should miss it when muted.
De-ess the send so the repeats do not spit.
questions.why: A delay repeats the consonants that carry intelligibility, so an unfiltered delay competes directly with the words it is repeating. Darkening it removes the consonants from the repeat while keeping the sense of space.
questions.watch: A dotted eighth delay lands on the next word at some tempos. Check at your actual BPM.

questions.q: What is a throw and how do I automate one?
questions.short: A burst of delay or reverb on one word, then gone. Automate the send, not the return.
steps: Pick the last word of a phrase, usually before a gap.
Automate the send up sharply for that word only, then straight back down.
Give the throw more feedback than the main delay so it tails away.
Let the repeats land in the silence, not under the next line.
Use them sparingly — two or three per song is a lot.
questions.why: A throw is loud enough to be an event and short enough not to interfere, which is only possible because the send is at zero everywhere else. Leaving the delay up at a safe permanent level gives you neither the event nor the clarity.
questions.watch: Automating the return instead of the send affects every source using that delay.

questions.q: How do I create depth without reverb?
questions.short: Level, high-frequency rolloff, and a single short delay. Those are the three cues the ear actually uses.
steps: Darken what should be further back: 2–3 dB off above 8 kHz reads as distance.
Compress what should be close and leave what should be far more dynamic.
Add a single filtered repeat at 60–120 ms rather than a tail.
Narrow the distant things and keep the close things wide or centred.
Lower the level last — it is the weakest of the four cues.
questions.why: Air absorbs high frequencies over distance, so a darker source is heard as further away regardless of its level. Reverb is only one of several distance cues, and in a dense mix it is the one that costs the most clarity.
questions.watch: Darkening everything to create depth leaves a mix with no top end and no front.

questions.q: What is the Haas effect and why is it risky?
questions.short: A delay under 35 ms on one side reads as width, not echo. It collapses badly in mono.
steps: Delay one side by 10–30 ms to widen a mono source.
Check mono immediately — this is the technique most likely to cancel.
Prefer a real double, a detuned copy or mid/side if either is available.
Never use it below 300 Hz.
If you use it, lower the delayed side 2–3 dB so mono summing is less destructive.
questions.why: Within about 35 ms the ear fuses two arrivals into one event and localises it toward whichever came first, which is why a short delay reads as position rather than echo. When summed to mono the two arrivals interfere instead, producing comb filtering across the whole spectrum.
questions.watch: Clubs and phone speakers are effectively mono. Haas-widened parts can disappear entirely there.

questions.q: Should delay be exactly in time or slightly off?
aliases: delay in time or off grid
questions.short: In time when it should be rhythmic, slightly off when it should be a texture.
steps: Sync to the grid for anything the listener should feel as rhythm.
Detune the time by 3–8 ms for a thickening effect that does not lock to the beat.
Use a non-obvious subdivision — dotted eighth or triplet — to avoid landing on the next hit.
On slower songs, slightly late repeats feel more human than exact ones.
Use the PulseRoom Delay page to get the exact value at your tempo, then adjust from there.
questions.why: A delay exactly on a subdivision reinforces the rhythm, which is useful when you want it heard. Pushed a few milliseconds off, the repeat no longer coincides with anything and becomes texture rather than an event.
questions.watch: An exact quarter-note delay often lands on the next word. Dotted eighth is the usual escape.

questions.q: What is mono compatibility and how do I check it?
aliases: does my mix work in mono
questions.short: Whether the mix survives being summed to one channel. Check often, and listen for things vanishing.
steps: Put a mono button on the master and use it every ten minutes.
Listen for anything that drops in level or disappears entirely.
Check the level difference between stereo and mono — more than 3 dB means trouble.
Suspect stereo wideners, Haas delays, and duplicated-then-delayed tracks first.
Keep everything below 120 Hz mono as a matter of course.
questions.why: Summing to mono adds the two channels, so anything present in both but out of phase cancels. Clubs, phone speakers, some Bluetooth devices and many broadcast paths are mono, which makes this a playback reality rather than a theoretical concern.
questions.watch: A mix can sound fine in mono and still have lost its hook. Listen for what left, not just whether it is worse.

questions.q: What is the difference between polarity and phase?
questions.short: Polarity is a simple flip, the same at every frequency. Phase is a time shift, different at each frequency.
steps: Use the polarity button first — it is instant and often fixes multi-mic problems entirely.
If flipping polarity helps but does not fix it, the issue is timing, not polarity.
For timing, nudge one track by samples until the summed low end is loudest.
Check every multi-mic source: kick in and out, snare top and bottom, DI and amp.
Judge by listening to the summed signal, not to either mic alone.
questions.why: Flipping polarity inverts the whole waveform, correcting a wiring or mic-orientation error. A phase difference comes from one source arriving later than another, so it affects each frequency by a different fraction of its cycle — which is why no single button fixes it.
questions.watch: The button labelled 'phase' on almost every console and plugin is actually polarity.

questions.q: What is comb filtering?
questions.short: Regular notches across the spectrum when a signal sums with a delayed copy of itself. Sounds hollow.
steps: Suspect it whenever two mics capture one source, or a copy is delayed.
Listen for a hollow, swirling, slightly metallic quality rather than an obvious problem.
Fix by aligning the timing, not by EQ — the notches are too many and too narrow.
Check mono, which is where comb filtering from stereo tricks becomes audible.
If it is deliberate, as in flanging, it is the same phenomenon used on purpose.
questions.why: A signal summed with a copy delayed by one millisecond cancels at 500 Hz, 1500 Hz, 2500 Hz and so on — evenly spaced notches whose pattern looks like a comb. EQ cannot restore them because the energy was cancelled, not attenuated.
questions.watch: Comb filtering from room reflections is why an untreated room makes every mix decision unreliable.

questions.q: How do I read a correlation meter?
questions.short: +1 is mono, 0 is wide, −1 cancels in mono. Live between 0 and +1 and you are safe.
steps: Keep the overall mix between +0.3 and +1 most of the time.
Treat anything sitting below 0 as a problem to investigate.
Check the low end separately; it should read close to +1.
Use it as a warning light, not a target — a reading of +1 means your mix is mono.
Always confirm with the mono button; the meter tells you where to look, not what it sounds like.
questions.why: Correlation measures how similar the two channels are. Identical channels read +1 and sum perfectly; inverted channels read −1 and cancel completely. Negative readings predict exactly what will vanish when a club system sums your mix.
questions.watch: Brief dips below zero are normal on wide reverb tails. Sustained negative readings are not.

questions.q: Should the low end be mono?
questions.short: Yes, below about 120 Hz. It costs nothing audible and protects against cancellation everywhere.
steps: Put a mono-maker on the mix bus set to 100–150 Hz.
Keep kick, bass and 808 centred and mono at the source as well.
Check the correlation meter reads near +1 in the low band.
Leave above 150 Hz alone — that is where your width lives.
Verify with the mono button that nothing disappears.
questions.why: The ear cannot localise frequencies below roughly 150 Hz, because the wavelengths are longer than the distance between your ears. Stereo information down there therefore carries no perceptual benefit, while costing headroom and risking cancellation on any system that sums.
questions.watch: Monoing too high, above 200 Hz, narrows guitars and keys and makes the mix feel smaller.

questions.q: What is mid/side processing?
questions.short: Splitting a stereo signal into what both channels share and what differs, then treating each separately.
steps: Use it to high-pass the sides while leaving the centre full-range.
Use it to cut presence from the mid so the vocal has room, without narrowing the mix.
Use it to add air to the sides only, for width without brightening the centre.
Keep moves small, 1–2 dB, and always check mono.
Do not use it to widen a mix that was not wide — it exaggerates, it does not create.
questions.why: Mid is the sum of the channels and side is their difference, so processing them separately lets you change the centre and the width independently. Because side is a difference signal, anything you do there is invisible in stereo and fully audible in mono.
questions.watch: Boosting the sides raises what cancels in mono. Check every move with the mono button.

questions.q: How wide is too wide?
questions.short: When mono costs you more than 2–3 dB, or when the centre feels hollow. Width is a contrast, not a goal.
steps: Compare stereo and mono levels. More than 3 dB of loss means too wide.
Keep kick, snare, bass and lead vocal centred — they are the anchor width is measured against.
If everything is wide, nothing sounds wide. Keep some things narrow deliberately.
Check on a phone speaker, which is mono and is where most listening happens.
Widen one or two elements a lot rather than everything a little.
questions.why: Width is perceived relative to what is narrow, so a mix where everything is spread has no reference and reads as vague rather than wide. The hollow centre that results is the most common symptom of over-widening.
questions.watch: Headphones flatter width enormously. A mix that feels right on headphones is usually too wide on speakers.

questions.q: How do I fix a phase problem between two mics?
questions.short: Flip polarity first. If that is not enough, nudge one track in samples until the low end is loudest.
steps: Flip the polarity on one mic and keep whichever sums louder.
If still thin, zoom in and nudge one track until the waveforms align at the transient.
Judge by the loudness of the summed low end, not by how the waveforms look.
Check the result against each mic soloed — the sum should be bigger than either.
On a full kit, align everything to the snare or the overheads, not pairwise.
questions.why: Two mics at different distances from one source receive it at different times, so some frequencies reinforce and others cancel. Polarity fixes a total inversion; a time nudge fixes a path-length difference, and they are different problems with different symptoms.
questions.watch: Aligning to one source can misalign from another. On a kit, pick what matters most and accept the rest.

questions.q: What is the 3:1 rule for mic placement?
questions.short: Put the second mic at least three times further from the first than the first is from its source.
steps: Measure the distance from mic one to its source.
Place mic two at least three times that distance away from mic one.
Apply it to choirs, drum kits, horn sections and anywhere mics share a room.
Check the result by listening to the pair summed, not individually.
When the rule is impossible, accept bleed and fix phase instead.
questions.why: At three times the distance the bleed arrives about 10 dB quieter than the direct sound, which is low enough that the comb filtering it causes is largely inaudible. It is a rule of thumb derived from the inverse square law, not a physical constant.
questions.watch: The rule reduces audible comb filtering; it does not eliminate bleed. Expect both on any live session.

questions.q: How do I widen something without a stereo widener?
questions.short: Two performances, different tones, or mid/side. All three survive mono; a widener does not.
steps: Record the part twice and pan the takes hard opposite. This is the best option by a long way.
If you only have one take, duplicate and change the tone substantially — different amp, different EQ.
Use mid/side to raise the side channel 2–3 dB above 300 Hz.
Pan the existing parts further apart before adding anything.
Check mono after each approach and keep the one that survives.
questions.why: Real width comes from genuine differences between the channels — in timing, pitch and timbre — which is what two performances give you. A widener manufactures difference with phase manipulation, and phase manipulation is exactly what mono summing undoes.
questions.watch: Duplicating a track and delaying one copy is the Haas trick, and it is the least mono-safe of these.

questions.q: What does saturation actually add?
questions.short: Harmonics above the original signal, plus gentle compression. It makes things louder without more level.
steps: Use it when something needs presence that EQ cannot supply — the content is not there to boost.
Expect it to add level; match gain before judging whether it helped.
Use it on bass and sub so the note is audible on speakers with no low end.
Drive it until you hear it, then back off until you only notice it bypassed.
Oversample it, or the harmonics will alias back into the mix as false tones.
questions.why: Saturation generates new frequencies mathematically related to what is already there, so unlike EQ it can create content where none existed. Because those harmonics follow the source, the added brightness tracks the performance instead of sitting statically on top of it.
questions.watch: Saturation also compresses. Stacking it with a compressor can squash more than you intended.

questions.q: Tape, tube, transistor or diode — what is the difference?
questions.short: Tape for glue and softened transients, tube for warmth, transistor for edge, diode for aggression.
steps: Tape: soft compression, rolled highs, thickened lows. Drum buses and mix buses.
Tube: even harmonics, warm and forgiving. Vocals, bass, keys.
Transistor: odd harmonics, harder edge. Snares, rock guitars, parallel channels.
Diode or clipper: hard and aggressive. Clipping drum peaks, rap vocals in parallel.
Try the same amount of each and keep whichever sits best — the names matter less than the result.
questions.why: Each circuit distorts asymmetrically or symmetrically in different ways, which determines whether it generates mostly even harmonics, heard as warmth and thickness, or odd ones, heard as edge and aggression. The tonal labels describe that harmonic signature.
questions.watch: Plugin emulations vary wildly in accuracy. Judge by ear, not by the name on the panel.

questions.q: When should I saturate instead of EQ?
questions.short: When the content you want is not there to boost. EQ amplifies, saturation creates.
steps: Brightening a dull source: saturate first, then shelf. The shelf has more to work with.
Making a sub audible on small speakers: saturation only. EQ cannot help.
Removing a resonance: EQ only. Saturation has no subtractive mode.
Adding presence to a close-miked source: either, but saturation keeps it dynamic.
Try both at matched gain and keep whichever you prefer.
questions.why: An equaliser scales what exists at a frequency, so where there is nothing it produces nothing but noise. Saturation derives new harmonics from the fundamental, so it can put energy in a band the source never occupied.
questions.watch: Saturation affects the whole signal, not one band. Use a filtered parallel path for targeted work.

questions.q: What is harmonic distortion doing to my low end?
questions.short: Putting the note's identity into bands that small speakers can actually reproduce.
steps: Saturate the bass or 808 and listen on a laptop with no sub response.
Check the second and third harmonics land in 100–300 Hz and are not cut there.
Keep a clean parallel path for the fundamental so monitors and clubs still get it.
Watch the low mids — saturation puts energy exactly where mud lives.
Judge it on the smallest speaker you own, not the largest.
questions.why: A 50 Hz note saturated produces energy at 100, 150 and 200 Hz. The ear reconstructs the pitch of a missing fundamental from that series, which is why a saturated bass has an audible note on a phone while an unsaturated one is silent there.
questions.watch: Those same harmonics are the mud you cut elsewhere. Cutting them on the bass undoes the benefit.

questions.q: How much saturation is too much?
questions.short: When you can identify it bypassed but not engaged, you are close. When it changes the instrument, you passed it.
steps: Match gain, then A/B. If the saturated version is obviously distorted, back off.
Drive it until it is clearly audible, then reduce by half.
Check on headphones; saturation hides on speakers and reveals itself in earbuds.
Watch for the low end losing weight — that is the first sign of too much.
Across a whole mix, many lightly saturated channels add up. Check the master.
questions.why: Saturation sounds better the more you add right up until it does not, and the transition is gradual rather than obvious. Judging it bypassed rather than engaged is the only reliable test, because your ear adapts to distortion within seconds.
questions.watch: Saturation on every channel is the most common cause of a mix that is loud, dense and tiring.

questions.q: What does mastering actually do?
aliases: what does a mastering engineer do
questions.short: Final tonal balance, loudness, consistency across a release, and delivery formats. Not fixing a mix.
steps: Expect broad tonal adjustment, 1–2 dB moves, not surgical correction.
Expect loudness and dynamics control for the target platform.
Expect consistency across every track on a release.
Expect correct formats, metadata, spacing and fades.
Do not expect it to fix a balance problem. That is a remix.
questions.why: Mastering works on a stereo file, so it can only change things that apply to everything at once. Anything requiring a single element to move is outside what the medium allows, which is why the honest answer to most mix problems at this stage is to go back.
questions.watch: A mastering engineer who says the mix needs work is giving you the most valuable note on the project.

questions.q: Can I master my own mix?
aliases: should I master my own mix
questions.short: Yes, but leave a day between finishing the mix and starting, and reference constantly.
steps: Finish the mix, then wait at least a day. Fresh ears are the thing you are missing.
Open a new session with only the bounced mix in it.
Work with two or three references, loudness-matched.
Keep moves small: 1–2 dB of EQ and 2–4 dB of limiting.
If you find yourself making a move bigger than 3 dB, go back and fix the mix.
questions.why: What a mastering engineer mainly brings is a second set of ears, a known room and no attachment to the decisions already made. You cannot buy the first two cheaply, but you can partly manufacture the third with time and references.
questions.watch: Mastering your own mix on the same day is just continuing to mix with fewer tools.

questions.q: What is stem mastering?
questions.short: Mastering from five or six grouped buses instead of one stereo file. More control, more responsibility.
steps: Deliver 5–8 stems: drums, bass, vocals, backing vocals, instruments, effects.
Export every stem from bar one at the session's sample rate, 24-bit.
Bypass the mix bus chain, or supply it separately with a note.
Check that the stems sum to your mix before sending them.
Expect it to cost more and take longer than stereo mastering.
questions.why: With stems a mastering engineer can change the relationship between elements, not just the overall tone, which allows fixes that are impossible on a stereo file. The cost is that they are now making mix decisions, which is work you were presumably paying them not to need.
questions.watch: Stems that do not sum back to your mix mean something in the chain is not being exported. Check first.

questions.q: How loud should my master be for each platform?
questions.short: −14 LUFS for streaming, −9 to −7 for club, −23 for broadcast, −16 for podcast. True peak −1.
steps: Spotify, Apple Music, YouTube, Tidal, Amazon: −14 LUFS integrated, −1 dBTP.
Club or DJ use: −9 to −7 LUFS. No normalisation on a PA.
Broadcast under EBU R128: −23 LUFS with ±0.5 LU tolerance.
Podcast and spoken word: −16 LUFS, mono-safe.
Measure integrated across the whole track, not over the chorus.
questions.why: Streaming targets are normalisation points, so exceeding them only loses dynamics. Broadcast targets are regulatory, set by EBU R128 and measured with ITU-R BS.1770. Club targets are neither — they exist because PA playback has no normalisation at all.
questions.watch: Platforms change their numbers occasionally. Check before a major release rather than trusting a chart.

questions.q: Should I leave the limiter off for the mastering engineer?
questions.short: Yes. But if it is part of the sound, send both versions and say which is which.
steps: Bounce one version with the mix bus limiter bypassed, peaking around −6 dBFS.
If you mixed into it and it shapes the sound, bounce a second version with it on.
Label them clearly: Title_NoLimiter and Title_Reference.
Keep any compression that is a creative choice; only the final limiter comes off.
Say in your notes what you were going for.
questions.why: A limiter removes the peak information a mastering engineer would use and leaves no headroom to work in. The exception is real: if the limiter is audibly part of the record's character, removing it changes the mix rather than just its level.
questions.watch: Sending only a limited file and asking for it to be made louder is asking for distortion.

questions.q: What order should a mastering chain go in?
questions.short: Corrective EQ, compression, tonal EQ, saturation, stereo, limiter, metering. Limiter always last.
steps: Subtractive EQ first: remove any resonance or excess before anything reacts to it.
Gentle compression next, 1–2 dB, for cohesion.
Tonal EQ after, for the broad character you want.
Saturation for density, then any stereo work.
Limiter last, then a meter after it that you only read, never adjust.
questions.why: Each stage changes what the next receives, so removing problems before compressing means the compressor responds to music rather than to a resonance. The limiter is last because everything before it adds level, and the limiter's job is to define the ceiling after all of that.
questions.watch: A mastering chain longer than five processors is usually compensating for a mix that is not finished.

questions.q: How do I know when a master is done?
questions.short: When it matches your references at the same loudness and nothing stands out on four systems.
steps: Loudness-match against two references and compare tonal balance, not level.
Check on monitors, headphones, a phone and a car.
Confirm the integrated LUFS and true peak hit your targets.
Listen to the whole track once without touching anything.
If your last three moves were lateral, stop.
questions.why: Mastering has a narrower goal than mixing — match a target and translate everywhere — so it has a clearer finish line. Once the measurements are met and nothing stands out across systems, further changes are preference rather than improvement.
questions.watch: Loudness is the easiest thing to keep chasing and the one with the least benefit. Hit the target and stop.

questions.q: How do I know if I have too much low end?
aliases: is my low end too much
questions.short: Compare to a reference at matched loudness, and check a phone. Your room is lying to you either way.
steps: Loudness-match a reference and switch between them listening only to the low end.
Check on a phone: if the mix sounds hollow there, the low end may be covering the mids.
Check in the car, where 60–120 Hz is exaggerated.
Use a spectrum analyser as a second opinion, not a first one.
If the mix gets quieter when you add low end, there is too much.
questions.why: Every untreated room has nulls and peaks below 300 Hz that can be 10 dB or more, so your perception of the low end is substantially a property of where you are sitting. References and small speakers both bypass that, which is why they are more trustworthy than careful listening.
questions.watch: Too much low end also eats loudness. If your limiter is working hard, suspect the bass first.

questions.q: How do I mix low end without a subwoofer?
questions.short: Use a spectrum analyser, headphones and references together. No single one of them is enough.
steps: Use a spectrum analyser to see what you cannot hear below your monitors' range.
Cross-check on headphones, which usually extend lower than small monitors.
Reference commercially released tracks constantly at matched loudness.
Keep everything below 120 Hz mono so you cannot create problems you cannot hear.
Check the car and a phone before you finish.
questions.why: A small monitor rolls off well above the fundamental of a kick or an 808, so the entire decision is being made on evidence you do not have. Measurement, headphones and references each supply a different part of that missing information.
questions.watch: An analyser shows energy, not whether it sounds good. Use it to catch what you cannot hear, not to decide.

questions.q: What is the difference between sub, bass and low mids?
questions.short: Sub 20–60 Hz is felt, bass 60–250 Hz is the note, low mids 250–500 Hz is weight and mud.
steps: Sub, 20–60 Hz: felt more than heard. Kick and 808 fundamentals. Keep it mono and controlled.
Bass, 60–250 Hz: where the note lives and where kick and bass compete.
Low mids, 250–500 Hz: body and warmth, and the most-cut region in mixing.
Diagnose by range: no weight is bass, no power is sub, cloudiness is low mids.
Treat them separately — one filter rarely addresses the right one.
questions.why: These bands behave differently acoustically and perceptually: sub is omnidirectional and felt, bass carries pitch, and low mids carry the body of almost every instrument at once. Lumping them together as 'the low end' is why so many low-end fixes make the wrong thing worse.
questions.watch: Most phones and laptops reproduce none of the first band and little of the second.

questions.q: How do I judge low end on headphones?
questions.short: Learn one pair over months, use an analyser alongside, and verify everything against references.
steps: Pick one pair and use them for everything until you know how they lie.
Keep an analyser open for anything below 60 Hz.
Reference constantly at matched loudness; your memory of a good low end is unreliable.
Check the fit — a poor seal changes low-end response by many decibels.
Confirm on speakers or in a car before finishing.
questions.why: Headphone low-frequency response depends on the seal between the cup and your head, which varies with fit, glasses and hair. That makes the absolute level unreliable even on accurate headphones — but the relative balance stays consistent once you know them.
questions.watch: Open-back headphones lose low end badly in a noisy room. The environment is part of the measurement.

questions.q: Why does my low end sound different in the car?
questions.short: A car is a small sealed box with a strong resonance around 60–120 Hz. It exaggerates, usefully.
steps: Use the car to check whether the low end is out of control, not to set its level.
Play a reference in the same car immediately before and after.
Fix only what is clearly excessive; do not mix to the car's response.
Use the same car every time, with the EQ flat and loudness off.
Drive — a stationary car with the engine off is not how anyone listens.
questions.why: A car cabin is small enough that its lowest resonant mode lands in the bass region, producing a large boost that varies with the specific vehicle. That exaggeration makes it a sensitive detector of excess low end and a poor guide to how much there should be.
questions.watch: Car systems often have loudness compensation on by default, which adds more bass again. Turn it off.
